top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits one coherent, jointly authored body of design-based evidence on how technology and trade shocks reshape labour demand and local adjustment. The work has run for over a decade and has been replicated in other countries and refined without being overturned. Dorn is a full co-author of the central import-shock papers, so naming him keeps the attribution accurate. The citation should claim credible evidence on adjustment, not settled welfare magnitudes or origination of the task framework. The cost is that it omits Katz's skill-premium framework, which P003 would credit. I put P003 second because it is a defensible variant that credits the framework more fully, but it has a more composite attribution and sits closer to ground recognised in 2023. P002 comes next because its methods are mature and widely validated, though it is a methods prize and Bresnahan and Reiss fall outside a three-name cap. P004 follows because the cross-country constitutional evidence is less credibly identified and Besley's share is the least separable. A no-award outcome is ranked last because several proposals rest on mature, important and well-attributed work.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, or the names on P002 and P004; none of her listed frequent co-authors is a candidate. Disclosed: she presented the 2023 Goldin prize, which is adjacent to Katz's earlier collaboration, and she works in labour economics, which is close to P001 and P003. This is disclosed, not adjudicated.
